title: AI policy must take into account democratic bargain
where: Editorial page, page 8 (Ruchi Gupta, executive director, Future of India Foundation)
syllabus: GS3 › Inclusive growth; employment · GS3 › Awareness in IT and emerging technology · GS2 › Government policies for development; vulnerable sections (youth) · Essay
summary: AI exposes fewer Indian jobs than in rich countries, yet India's development model is more vulnerable; the author proposes an AI and Work Observatory, apprenticeships, portable social protection and a parliamentary committee.
ideas: Three vulnerabilities: IT and entry-level cognitive work built India's middle class and consuming class; India has the world's largest youth population; and rich-country tools like UBI or public stakes in AI firms are not available.
GS3 · Employment / technology
AI threatens the very ladder, entry-level IT work, that built India's post-1991 middle class.
The broken pipeline: routine tasks AI now does are how inexperienced workers become experienced; cutting junior hiring weakens tomorrow's professionals.
GS3 · Skilling / labour market
If AI does junior work, the pipeline that produces senior professionals dries up.
Growth without jobs: offshored coding and support may move back in-house with AI; YouthPOWER analysis shows software exports growing while employment and real earnings weaken.
GS3 · Jobless growth
Software exports rising while jobs and real earnings fall is AI-era jobless growth.

Policy response: a national AI and Work Observatory; paid sectoral apprenticeships; human review of automated workplace decisions; portable social protection; a parliamentary committee hearing young people, workers, small firms and states.
GS2 · Policy design / participatory governance
Workers and young people must have a voice in setting the terms of AI adoption.
Demand for labour: 90% of young workers earn under Rs 20,000 a month; public investment in health, care, education, housing and urban services can create work where needs are unmet.
GS3 · Inclusive growth
Skilling improves access to work; only demand creates new work, through public investment in care and services.
keywords: The expectation that effort can improve one's circumstances, which sustains faith in democracy
AI policy must protect the democratic bargain: that effort leads to a better life.
Benefits that move with workers across jobs and employers
Portable social protection is the safety net for an AI-disrupted, job-hopping workforce.
Junior roles through which workers gain experience
AI's real threat is to the entry-level pipeline, not just to existing jobs.
Meaningful human review of automated decisions
Workers should have a human in the loop when algorithms decide on hiring or firing.
data: 90% (85% all ages)
Share of young Indian workers earning less than Rs 20,000 a month
Ruchi Gupta, The Indian Express
GS3 · Wages and employment
Ninety per cent of young Indian workers earn under Rs 20,000 a month, which limits demand and hiring.
examples: Work as dignity
Work gives competence, independence, social standing and a stake in the future
GS4
GS3 · Employment · GS4 · Dignity of labour
Work gives people competence, independence and standing, so an AI strategy must be judged by the work it creates.
pyqs: Linkages between education, skill and employment.
Fourth Industrial Revolution making e-governance integral to government.

trend.t: Employment questions moved from schemes (Make in India, Skill India, 2015) to the quality of growth: productivity-led job creation (2022), structural unemployment and the education–skill–job link (2023). AI entered as a technology question (agentic AI, 2026); the essay paper asked about AI and jobs in 2019.
trend.watch: AI was asked in 2026 as technology and jobs questions recur every year, so the overlap, AI's effect on entry-level work and on youth, is a likely next question.
focus: AI and the entry-level job ladder
Social protection for gig and AI-era workers
Demand-side job creation in care and services

potential: "India must judge its AI strategy by whether it expands access to productive work and upward mobility." Discuss. (15 marks)
How does artificial intelligence threaten the entry-level job pipeline in India? Suggest policy measures. (10 marks)

practice.q: "India must judge its AI strategy by whether it expands access to productive work and upward mobility." Discuss.
parts: Why AI is a particular risk for India

answer.t: Fewer Indian jobs are directly exposed to AI than in advanced economies, yet India's development model, built on IT services and a young workforce, is more vulnerable.

answer.h: Why AI is a particular risk for India

pts.t: IT and entry-level cognitive work created India's consuming class after liberalisation.
pts.ex: Disruption would spread to sectors that depend on their spending.

pts.t: The world's largest youth population needs productive jobs, unlike ageing economies.
pts.ex: Graduate unemployment is higher than for young people as a whole.

pts.t: Routine tasks are how juniors learn; firms may hire fewer of them.
pts.ex: Seniors retained to review AI work while junior hiring falls.

pts.t: Work once outsourced to India may be done in-house with AI.
pts.ex: Software exports grow while employment and real earnings weaken (YouthPOWER).

pts.t: UBI or public equity in AI firms are not options.
pts.ex: Fiscal limits on universal transfers.

pts.t: Depressed wages limit consumption and hiring.
pts.ex: 90% of young workers earn under Rs 20,000 a month.

pts.t: AI can widen access to scarce expertise.
pts.ex: AI-assisted diagnosis in rural clinics.

pts.t: AI tools can strengthen MSMEs.
pts.ex: Bookkeeping and marketing automation.

pts.t: Better delivery of education and health.
pts.ex: Personalised learning tools.

pts.t: A national AI and Work Observatory tracking entry-level hiring, wages and progression.
pts.ex: Policies that respond only to layoffs miss those never hired.

pts.t: Supervised work using AI on real problems.
pts.ex: Generic AI certificates cannot replace domain knowledge.

pts.t: Human review of automated workplace decisions; portable social protection.
pts.ex: Social Security Code coverage.

pts.t: A parliamentary committee hearing youth, workers, small firms and states.
pts.ex: Alongside technology companies.

pts.t: Public investment in health, care, education, housing and urban services.
pts.ex: Unmet needs are large.

pts.t: Higher earnings lift consumption and hiring.
pts.ex: Minimum wage and productivity links.

answer.t: Higher productivity will be a limited achievement if the routes through which young Indians share in it keep narrowing; AI policy is, in the end, employment policy.

title: Next on nation's to-do list: More productive jobs
where: Ideas page, page 9 (Tejasvi Surya, BJP MP, and Kishen Shastry, University of Cambridge); HSBC report on Economy page, page 13
syllabus: GS3 › Inclusive growth; employment; mobilisation of resources · GS2 › Welfare schemes and delivery (DBT) · GS2 › Fiscal federalism · Essay
summary: The authors credit India's sharp fall in extreme poverty to growth, state capacity and DBT, and say the next task is productive jobs through state-level reforms, which is at risk from states' subsidy burden.
evolution: World Bank: extreme poverty falls to 2.6% in 2023 (poverty thread).
Editorial: the challenge is more productive employment.
Two Ideas-page pieces on the same World Bank brief; HSBC flags falling real rural wages.
ideas: Additive and subtractive reform: unlike Reagan or Thatcher, India had to build basic state capacity (toilets, bank accounts, IDs, roads, ports) while reforming institutions (GST, IBC), facing 19th- and 21st-century problems at once.
GS2 · Governance / GS3 · Reforms
India's reform has been additive and subtractive: building the state's reach while removing barriers.

Poverty decline, as per the World Bank: extreme poverty fell from 27.1% (2011) to 2.6% (2023), and close to 50 crore people crossed the lower-middle-income line, credited to consumption growth, rising employment (especially women) and social transfers.
GS3 · Poverty / inclusive growth
Extreme poverty fell from 27.1% to 2.6% between 2011 and 2023, according to the World Bank.
Delivery architecture: DBT was revived and scaled on identity, bank accounts and payment rails across hundreds of schemes, cutting leakages; digital public infrastructure enabled social protection.
GS2 · E-governance / welfare delivery
DBT on Aadhaar, Jan Dhan and payment rails turned leaky subsidies into direct transfers.

The next frontier lies with states: reforms in power, land, urban planning and agricultural markets are in state hands, but states spend over Rs 3 lakh crore on subsidies, and with salaries, pensions and interest, over 90% of revenue receipts.
GS2 · Fiscal federalism / GS3 · Fiscal policy
Productive jobs need state reforms, but subsidies and committed spending leave states little fiscal space.
Counterpoint: HSBC says falling real rural wages 'cannot be ignored', with investment intentions rising only in value terms; job quality, not just poverty counts, is the real test.
GS3 · Employment and wages
Poverty is down, but falling real rural wages show that productive jobs remain the unfinished task.
keywords: The ability of the state to deliver services and enforce policy
The last decade showed India can build state capacity at scale; the next must sustain reform across states.
Room in a budget for new spending after committed expenditure
Subsidies eat the fiscal space states need for reforms that create jobs.
Salaries, pensions and interest that a government must pay
When committed expenditure and subsidies exceed 90% of revenue, capital spending suffers.
A state focused on building infrastructure at speed (from the book Breakneck)
India combines the ambition of an engineering state with the checks of a multiparty democracy.
data: Extreme poverty in India, 2011 to 2023 ($3/day, 2021 PPP)
World Bank India Poverty and Equity Brief, October 2026
GS3 · Poverty

~50 crore
People who moved above the lower-middle-income poverty line, 2011–2023

Close to 50 crore Indians moved above the lower-middle-income poverty line in 12 years.
examples: Karnataka's subsidy bill
Over Rs 1 lakh crore budgeted for subsidies, close to a third of revenue receipts (authors' figure)
GS3 · State finances
Karnataka's subsidy bill, about a third of its revenue, shows how welfare can crowd out investment.
DBT for cooking gas
Started reluctantly, abandoned before 2014, then revived and scaled
GS4
GS2 · Welfare delivery · GS4 · Good governance

Managing inflation and unemployment to serve the poor, beyond welfare schemes.

trend.t: Poverty questions moved from measurement (MPI, 2020) to the limits of welfare (beyond schemes, 2022; DBT limitations, 2022) and inequality (paradox of poverty, 2025); state finances entered with the Fiscal Health Index (2025).
trend.watch: The 2022 and 2025 questions both asked what lies beyond welfare transfers, so productive jobs and state fiscal health are likely angles.

potential: "India has shown it can reduce poverty through state capacity; it must now show it can create productive jobs." Discuss. (15 marks)

title: Tamil Nadu tightens grip on women-led electronics manufacturing
syllabus: GS1 › Role of women; Population and migration · GS3 › Employment; Industrial policy (manufacturing) · GS2 › Welfare of vulnerable sections; best practices in governance · GS4 › Innovation in public service; gender justice
summary: Annual Survey of Industries data for 2024-25 show Tamil Nadu employs 40.3% of all directly employed women factory workers in India and 44.4% of those making computer, electronic and optical products, helped by dormitories near factories.
evolution: Govt to study hurdles faced by women-led informal businesses (women and work thread).
Physicists bring STEM to women and rural youth.
ideas: Concentration of women's factory work: Tamil Nadu's share of directly employed women making computer, electronic and optical products rose from 42.9% to 44.4% in 2024-25; it employs 40.3% of all directly employed women factory workers in India.
GS1 · Women and work / GS3 · Manufacturing
Tamil Nadu employs two in five of India's directly employed women factory workers: proof that state policy shapes women's work.

A policy innovation that removes the real barriers: the two key obstacles for women are distance from work and living arrangements, and Tamil Nadu adapted China's model of dormitories for women workers.
GS4 · Innovation in public service / GS2 · Best practices
Tamil Nadu's factory dormitories are an innovation that solves women's real constraints, safety and distance, rather than offering only jobs.

Migration and an ageing south: southern states with ageing populations rely on migrant workers, so housing near factories is a key policy intervention; most surveyed migrants in the Chennai region came from Bihar, Odisha, Assam, UP and Jharkhand.
GS1 · Migration and demography
As the south ages and draws migrant workers from the east, worker housing becomes core industrial infrastructure.

A wide gender gap remains: directly employed women factory workers rose by 96,907 to 17.38 lakh, while men rose by 4.54 lakh to 78.78 lakh; Gujarat's share of women in electronics fell from 10% to 7.4%.
GS1 · Gender gap / GS3 · Employment
Women remain a small minority of India's factory workforce, so gains in one state must spread nationally.
A blind spot in the data: the survey gives no gender break-up of 70.31 lakh contract workers, so the true number of women in factories cannot be known.
GS3 · Employment data / GS2 · Statistics
Without gender data on contract workers, policy for women in factories is made half-blind.
keywords: Housing, transport, safety and childcare that let women take up jobs
Enabling infrastructure, not just job creation, decides whether women join the factory workforce.
Adapting a policy that worked elsewhere to local conditions
Tamil Nadu's dormitory model is policy transfer done well: borrowing the idea, adapting it to local needs.
Rising share of women in factory work, as in East Asian electronics
Electronics assembly can drive the feminisation of Indian manufacturing, as it did in East Asia.
Statistics broken down by sex to show gaps
Gender-disaggregated data on contract workers is the first step to gender-responsive labour policy.
Growing use of contract rather than directly employed workers
Contractualisation hides women workers from the statistics and from labour protections.

answer.t: Jobs open the factory door, but housing, safety and care let women walk through it; Tamil Nadu shows that a simple idea can turn women's potential into India's manufacturing strength.

title: Companies may be selective, but pvt capex picking up: FM
syllabus: GS3 › Indian economy: growth, development and employment; Industrial policy (MSMEs, PLI); Investment · GS2 › Government policies and interventions; Governance · GS4 › Trust and public service values in governance
summary: The Finance Minister said private investment is picking up selectively after the GST 2.0 reforms, MSMEs are being helped to grow through a new definition, and the PLI scheme's weaker sectors will be examined, with trust in citizens as the government's charter.
evolution: Jan Vishwas and trust-based reforms: the challenge is wages, not jobs.
Editorial: the challenge is more productive employment.
FM: MSMEs must grow from micro to large; policy built on trusting people.
ideas: Demand-led investment revival: the FM said GST 2.0 reforms made consumption and demand visible, so industry is investing again, though selectively in chosen sectors.
GS3 · Investment / Growth
Private capex follows visible demand: consumption recovery is the trigger for a sustained investment cycle.
Micro should not remain dwarfs: the revised MSME definition lets micro firms grow into small, small into medium and medium into large while keeping benefits.
GS3 · MSMEs / Industrial policy
Removing the penalty on growth helps India fill its 'missing middle' of mid-sized firms.
Beyond a few big firms: the FM rejected the view that a few large groups dominate the economy, citing flourishing MSMEs and fast-growing startups and unicorns.
GS3 · Industry structure
A broad base of MSMEs and startups, not a few conglomerates, makes growth inclusive and resilient.
Incentives tied to performance: PLI pays only for additional production; it has worked, but sectors that underperformed will be examined.
GS3 · Industrial policy (PLI)
Linking incentives to output, and reviewing failures, keeps industrial policy accountable.
Trust as the charter of governance: GST, income tax and other policies are framed on trusting businesses, farmers, taxpayers and citizens, with active, continuous dialogue with industry.
GS2 · Governance / GS4 · Trust
A trust-based state treats citizens as partners, cutting compliance burden and building cooperation.
keywords: Too few mid-sized firms between many tiny ones and a few large ones
India's missing middle keeps productivity low; helping MSMEs scale up is the cure.
Loss of benefits that deters a firm from growing beyond a size limit
A revised MSME definition removes the graduation penalty that kept firms small.
Clarity about future demand that gives firms confidence to invest
Visible consumption demand, not tax breaks alone, revives private capex.
Policy that presumes citizens are honest and reduces control
Trust-based governance shifts the state from suspicion to facilitation.
Support paid only on measurable output
Performance-linked incentives make public money pay only for results.

GS3 · MSMEs / Exports
MSMEs account for about 40% of India's exports (Finance Minister), so their growth is export growth.

The revised MSME definition shows how policy can reward growth instead of penalising it.
PLI's performance condition

'We trust the taxpayer'

focus: MSMEs: scaling up and the missing middle

parts: Measures to help them scale up

answer.t: MSMEs produce about 40% of India's exports (Finance Minister, Nov 2026), yet most stay micro; the government says it wants micro firms to grow into small, medium and large ones.

pts.t: Firms lose subsidies, reservations and tax benefits once they cross size limits, so they stay small.
pts.ex: The revised definition aims to remove this.

pts.t: Lack of collateral and formal records limits access to bank loans.
Large buyers and governments pay late, choking working capital.
Many inspections, filings and licences cost more for small firms.
pts.ex: Jan Vishwas decriminalisation is a response.

pts.t: Old machines and untrained workers keep productivity low.
Many firms stay outside the formal system to avoid tax and regulation.
Tiny firms cannot reach economies of scale.
Most employment is informal and low-paid.
pts.ex: Link: 'the challenge is wages, not jobs' (IE, 2 Nov).

pts.t: Few firms are large enough to supply global value chains.
A few large groups dominate while the base stays weak.

answer.h: Measures to help them scale up

pts.t: Let firms keep benefits for a period after crossing thresholds.
pts.ex: Revised MSME definition.

pts.t: Lend on digital transaction records, not just collateral.
pts.ex: TReDS for invoice discounting; CGTMSE credit guarantees.

pts.t: Penalise late payments to MSMEs.
Self-certification, fewer inspections, decriminalised minor offences.
pts.ex: FM: policy built on trusting business.

pts.t: Common facilities, testing labs and tool rooms for MSME clusters.

pts.k: Link to big firms and PLI
pts.t: Bring MSMEs into supply chains of large manufacturers and incentive schemes.
pts.ex: PLI rewards additional production.

pts.t: Apprenticeships and easy registration bring firms into the formal economy.
pts.ex: Udyam registration.

answer.t: India will become a manufacturing power only when its micro firms are free and able to grow; trust, credit and a growth-friendly policy can fill the missing middle.

title: The challenge is more productive employment
syllabus: GS3 › Inclusive growth; Employment; Growth and development · GS1 › Poverty; Role of women; Migration · GS2 › Issues relating to poverty
summary: With extreme poverty down to 2.6%, the editorial argues the next obstacle to mass prosperity is the lack of productive, better-paid non-farm jobs.
evolution: World Bank: extreme poverty falls to 2.6% in 2023; poverty concentrated in the UP–West Bengal belt (front page).
Manish Sabharwal: 'Challenge is wages, not jobs' (editorial page).
Editorial: the challenge is more productive employment.
ideas: Poverty fell, productivity did not follow: extreme poverty is down to 2.6% and the $4.2 line to 16.1%, but the lack of productive, better-paid non-farm jobs now blocks mass prosperity.
GS3 · Inclusive growth
India's next development challenge is not poverty reduction alone but productive employment.
More workers, not better work: labour force participation has risen, mostly as women join, but many are in farming or self-employment.
GS3 · Employment / GS1 · Women
Rising participation driven by women in farm and self-employment adds workers without raising productivity.
Stalled structural transformation: agriculture still employs a large share of workers compared with China and Vietnam, and most non-farm workers are in informal, low-productivity firms.
GS3 · Structural transformation
India's workforce has not moved out of farming at the pace East Asian economies managed.
Manufacturing missed its role: unlike other Asian economies, Indian manufacturing has not absorbed low-skilled workers; jobs grew in low-end services instead.
GS3 · Industrial policy
Without labour-intensive manufacturing, workers leaving farms crowd into low-end services.
Geography of jobs: poverty is concentrated in the UP–West Bengal belt, where incomes and jobs are scarce, so migration to richer regions is the main route to non-farm work.
GS1 · Migration / Regional disparity
Regional job deserts make migration the default escape route from poverty.
keywords: Shift of workers from low- to high-productivity sectors
Moving up the income ladder requires structural transformation of the workforce.
Manufacturing peaking early, before absorbing surplus labour
India shows signs of premature deindustrialisation, with services absorbing low-skilled labour.
Growth stalling before reaching high income
Low-productivity jobs risk trapping India below upper-middle income.
Moving for work because local options are absent
Job scarcity in the eastern belt drives distress migration.
Industries employing many low-skilled workers per unit of capital
Labour-intensive manufacturing is the missing bridge from farm to formal work.

answer.t: Extreme poverty is down to 2.6% (World Bank), yet only 21.68% of China's and 25% of Vietnam's workers are in farming, far below India, because Indian manufacturing has not absorbed surplus labour.

title: Challenge is wages, not jobs. Expanding Jan Vishwas interventions can help
where: The Editorial Page, page 8 (Manish Sabharwal, Teamlease Services)
syllabus: GS3 › Employment; Growth and development · GS2 › Government policies; Transparency and accountability; Citizen-centric governance · GS4 › Probity in governance
summary: After decriminalising thousands of offences, the writer argues the next Jan Vishwas phase should make every rule published, knowable and trust-based, because India's problem is low wages, not a lack of jobs.
ideas: Wages, not jobs: India's problem is job quality, not quantity; a third of the workforce is in employed poverty, trapped in informal wage work and self-employment.
GS3 · Employment
India's employment challenge is low-wage informality, not joblessness; the fix lies in formal, high-wage job creation.
Regulatory cholesterol: China's per-capita GDP is five times India's (on par in 1991), not because of effort but because of India's lack of transparency, consistency and trust in law enforcement.
GS3 · Growth / GS2 · Governance
Regulatory cholesterol, not lack of talent or effort, explains much of India's per-capita income gap with China.

Six toxic thought worlds: prior approval (prohibited till permitted), enforcing the unenforceable, process as punishment, blindness to 25+ instruments below Acts, laws for edge cases, and excessive criminalisation.
GS2 · Administrative reform
India's regulatory mindset (prior approval, process as punishment, over-criminalisation) treats the citizen as a suspect.

Three next steps: Siddhant (trust-based regulation on freedom, necessity, proportionality, adopted by 30 million+ civil servants), Sangreh (a single legal record as DPI) and Ashwasan (only published obligations are enforceable).
GS2 · Citizen-centric governance
Jan Vishwas must move from decriminalisation to trust, knowability and certainty through Siddhant, Sangreh and Ashwasan.

Law must be knowable: ignorance of law is no excuse only if the State makes law accessible; earlier attempts failed on design, capacity, fragmented power, attention and technology, and lacked a binding duty to publish.
GS2 · Rule of law / Transparency
A citizen's duty to obey the law presupposes the State's duty to publish it; unpublished rules breed uncertainty and corruption.
keywords: Accumulated rules, filings and permissions that clog enterprise
Regulatory cholesterol raises the cost of formality and pushes firms into informality.
Employed poverty shows India's real problem is wage quality, not job quantity.
A prohibited-till-permitted regime presumes guilt and slows enterprise.
The procedure itself harasses the innocent
When process is punishment, even compliant citizens bear the cost of regulation.
Ignorance of the law is no excuse
Ignorantia juris holds only when the State makes the law knowable.
One machine-readable source for every legal obligation (Sangreh)
A legal DPI like Sangreh can do for compliance what UPI did for payments.
examples: Supreme Court on knowable law
Harla v State of Rajasthan (1952) rejected secret laws; B K Srinivasan (1987) moved to knowability; Viraj Impex (2019) held law operative only when published
GS2 · Judiciary / Rule of law
From Harla (1952) to Viraj Impex (2019), courts have held unpublished law cannot bind citizens.
Global single-source registers
US Federal Register, UK legislation.gov.uk, EU EUR-Lex, Singapore Statutes Online
GS2 · Comparative governance
Democracies like the US, UK and Singapore publish all binding rules in one register; India's Sangreh can follow.
Transparency of Rules Act (TORA)
Sanjeev Sanyal's draft: every enforceable obligation must be published on Sangreh
GS4
GS2 · Transparency / GS4 · Probity
TORA would make publication a precondition for enforcement, curbing discretion and corruption.
Adam Smith and the Constitution
250 years of The Wealth of Nations, 76 of the Constitution: both see government as expanding freedom
GS2 · Constitutional values / Essay
Both Adam Smith and the Constitution see the State as an enabler of freedom, not its gatekeeper.

answer.t: Jan Vishwas has decriminalised thousands of offences, yet a third of India's workforce remains in employed poverty, held back by regulatory cholesterol.

pts.t: The State treats citizens and firms as honest stakeholders, not suspects.
Fewer jail terms for minor lapses reduce the fear of becoming formal.
Less 'process is punishment' lets firms combine land, labour and capital.
Less discretion means fewer chances for rent-seeking.
Fewer petty cases clog courts.
It attacks the root of informality.
Freedom, necessity and proportionality to guide regulation, adopted by 30 million+ civil servants.
One machine-readable legal DPI, unifying gazettes and India Code.
Only published obligations should be enforceable.
Periodic pruning of circulars and rules.

answer.t: Jan Vishwas must move from decriminalisation to certainty, so that what is wrong with India's regulation is fixed by what is right with its democracy.

title: How welfare board will function, what changes for unorganised, gig workers
where: Economy, page 10 (Ravi Dutta Mishra & Aanchal Magazine)
syllabus: GS3 › Employment; Labour reforms · GS2 › Welfare schemes for vulnerable sections; Statutory bodies
summary: Follow-up: the Labour Ministry has notified two social security boards (40 members for unorganised workers, 22 for gig and platform workers) under the Code on Social Security.
evolution: Labour Ministry notifies the National Social Security Board under the Code on Social Security (Economy, page 23).
Details: two boards, aggregator contributions to a social security fund, and EPFO coverage widened.
ideas: Two boards, not one: a 40-member board for unorganised workers and a 22-member board for gig and platform workers, which includes aggregators such as quick-commerce and delivery platforms.
GS2 · Statutory bodies
Separate boards recognise that gig and platform workers need schemes designed for platform work.
Who pays: aggregators must contribute 1–2% of annual turnover to a social security fund, capped at 5% of what they pay workers; the fund also draws on governments, CSR and fines.
GS3 · Labour / GS2 · Welfare
Aggregator contributions put part of the cost of gig workers' security on the platforms that profit from them.
What it covers: schemes for life and disability cover, accident insurance, health and maternity benefits, old-age protection and crèches.
GS2 · Welfare
Social security for gig workers spans life-cycle risks, from maternity to old age.
Wider formal coverage: EPFO provisions now apply to all establishments with 20 or more employees, regardless of industry, not only those in the old schedule.
GS3 · Labour reforms
Extending EPFO to all establishments with 20+ workers widens formal social security.
keywords: Pooled fund for unorganised, gig and platform workers
A dedicated Social Security Fund gives gig workers' schemes a stable financing base.
Platforms paying a share of turnover towards workers' welfare
The aggregator levy shares the cost of social protection with platforms.
